titel: Wirecard: The €1.9 Billion That Never Existed | Documentary
beschreibung:
In June 2020, auditors asked Germany's tech champion a simple question: where is the money? The answer brought down a DAX company worth more than Deutsche Bank, exposed a regulator that went after journalists instead of fraudsters, and sent one executive on the run to Moscow.

abschnitte.text: In June 2020, a team of auditors asked one of Germany's most celebrated companies a very simple question. Where is the money? Not a little money. One point nine billion euros. A quarter of the entire balance sheet.

bilder.unter: a quarter of the balance sheet

abschnitte.text: The money was supposed to sit in two banks in the Philippines. The banks said they had never seen it. Within one week, a company that had been worth more than Deutsche Bank was bankrupt. Its chief executive was under arrest. And its second most powerful manager had disappeared.

This is the story of Wirecard. A story about greed, about a regulator that protected the wrong side, and about a man who, according to investigators, ended up in Moscow. And the strangest part? The warnings were there for years.

Wirecard was founded in 1999 near Munich, at the height of the dot com boom. Its business sounded boring. It processed card payments for online shops. But in the early years, some of its most important customers were in two industries that banks preferred not to touch. Online gambling, and adult websites.

In 2002, an Austrian IT consultant named Markus Braun became chief executive. He liked black turtlenecks and big visions. He talked about artificial intelligence, about the future of money, about a world without cash. Investors loved it.

Next to him rose a much younger manager. Jan Marsalek, also Austrian, joined in 2000 without a university degree and became chief operating officer in 2010. He was responsible for the fast growing business in Asia and the Middle East. He travelled constantly. And he collected contacts, not only in business.

In 2005 Wirecard went public through the back door, by taking over an already listed shell company. From then on, the numbers only went one way. Up. Revenue, profits, acquisitions in India, in Singapore, in Indonesia.

In September 2018, Wirecard reached the top. It joined the DAX, Germany's index of its thirty largest listed companies. It replaced Commerzbank. For a moment, the payment processor from a suburb of Munich was worth more than Deutsche Bank. Around twenty four billion euros.

Germany finally had what it had been missing for years. A tech champion. A company that could stand next to the giants from Silicon Valley. And because everyone wanted that story to be true, very few people wanted to hear that it might not be.

The first doubts came early. As far back as 2008, a German shareholder association raised questions about Wirecard's accounts. The company fought back hard. And the critics were attacked, not the company.

In 2015, the Financial Times published a series called House of Wirecard. Journalists Dan McCrum and Paul Murphy asked a basic question. Why did the numbers from Wirecard's Asian business not seem to add up? Short sellers, investors who bet on falling share prices, started to dig as well.

bilder.archiv: File:Financial Times building One Southwark Bridge.jpg

abschnitte.text: Each time, Wirecard had an answer. The critics were speculators, it said. They wanted to drive down the share price to make money. Some investors believed the company, others believed the journalists. The share price kept rising.

Then, in January 2019, the Financial Times reported something much more concrete. A whistleblower inside Wirecard's office in Singapore had raised alarm. Internal documents pointed to suspected forgery and backdating of contracts. The share price crashed.

bilder.zitat: Suspected forgery and backdating of contracts in Wirecard's Singapore office.

abschnitte.text: This should have been the moment when everyone looked closer. Instead, Germany did something that is still hard to believe today.

On the eighteenth of February 2019, Germany's financial regulator BaFin banned new bets against Wirecard shares. For two months, short selling was forbidden. It was the first time BaFin had ever done this for a single company.

The message to the market was clear. Wirecard is the victim here. And the regulator went even further. In April 2019, BaFin filed a criminal complaint. Not against Wirecard's managers. Against the journalists of the Financial Times, and against short sellers, on suspicion of market manipulation.
Think about that for a second. The journalists who were asking where the money was, were investigated. The company they were asking about, joined the most important stock index in the country.
The case against the journalists was later dropped. But it had sent a signal. In Germany, criticising Wirecard was risky. And inside Wirecard, the numbers kept growing.

By late 2019, the Financial Times published internal spreadsheets. They suggested that a large share of Wirecard's profits came from just three partner companies, in Dubai, Singapore and Manila. Under pressure, Wirecard hired the auditing firm KPMG for a special investigation. It was supposed to clear the company's name once and for all.

On the twenty eighth of April 2020, the KPMG report came out. It did not clear Wirecard. KPMG wrote that it could not verify that the revenue from those partner businesses between 2016 and 2018 was real. Wirecard, it said, had not provided the necessary documents. The share price fell by a quarter in one day.

bilder.zitat: KPMG could not verify the existence of the revenue from the third-party partner business for 2016 to 2018.

abschnitte.text: Then came the eighteenth of June 2020. Wirecard's long time auditor, EY, refused to sign the annual accounts. The reason: one point nine billion euros, supposedly held in trust accounts at two banks in the Philippines, could not be confirmed. The bank confirmations, Wirecard itself admitted, may have been fake.

bilder.zitat: There are indications that spurious balance confirmations were provided in order to deceive the auditor.

abschnitte.text: The share price collapsed by more than sixty percent in a single day. The next morning, Markus Braun resigned. The two Philippine banks said the documents were not theirs. And the governor of the Philippine central bank said the money had never even entered the country's financial system.
On the twenty second of June, Wirecard gave up. In a short statement, the company said what had been unthinkable just weeks before.

bilder.zitat: There is a prevailing likelihood that the bank trust account balances in the amount of EUR 1.9 billion do not exist.

abschnitte.text: That evening, Markus Braun turned himself in to prosecutors in Munich. He was released on bail, then arrested again a month later. On the twenty fifth of June 2020, Wirecard filed for insolvency. It was the first company in the history of the DAX to go bankrupt.

bilder.unter: first DAX company ever to go bankrupt

abschnitte.text: Billions of euros in savings were gone. Small investors who had trusted the German tech champion lost almost everything. Banks that had lent Wirecard money were left with huge holes. And one question became more urgent every hour. Where was Jan Marsalek?

Wirecard suspended Marsalek on the eighteenth of June and fired him a few days later. By then, he was already gone. According to investigators and multiple media reports, on the nineteenth of June he boarded a private plane at a small airfield in Austria. Its destination was Minsk, in Belarus.

His name went onto Europe's most wanted lists. But the trail went cold. Over the following years, journalists pieced together a picture that sounded more like a spy novel than a finance story. Marsalek, they reported, had long-standing contacts to Russian intelligence.

In 2025, a court in London convicted members of a Bulgarian spy ring that had spied on journalists and others across Europe. According to British prosecutors, the group took its orders from Jan Marsalek.

bilder.unter: spy ring convicted · orders allegedly from Marsalek

abschnitte.text: In September 2025, an investigation by Der Spiegel and other media outlets reported that Marsalek was living in Moscow under a false identity, apparently working with Russian intelligence. Russia has not commented on his whereabouts. German authorities still have an arrest warrant out for him.
Think about what that means. For years, one of the top managers of a company in Germany's most important stock index may have had ties to a foreign intelligence service. And nobody in charge noticed.

After the collapse, the German parliament set up a committee of inquiry. For months it questioned regulators, auditors, ministers and managers. Among the witnesses was the finance minister at the time, Olaf Scholz.

The conclusions were damning. BaFin had treated Wirecard mainly as a technology company and not as a financial group. It had looked at the critics instead of the company. The president of BaFin had to leave in January 2021. The regulator was reorganised.

And the auditors? EY had signed off on Wirecard's accounts for years. In 2023, Germany's auditor oversight body sanctioned EY Germany, with a fine and a two year ban on taking on new audit clients of public interest, such as listed companies.

bilder.unter: 2023 · two-year ban on new listed clients

abschnitte.text: In December 2022, the criminal trial against Markus Braun and two other former managers began in Munich. Prosecutors accuse him of fraud, breach of trust and market manipulation. Braun denies everything. He says he was the victim of a gang around Marsalek. One of his co-defendants, the former head of the Dubai business, became the key witness for the prosecution.

bilder.archiv: File:Aerial image of the Augsburg-Gablingen prison (view from the southeast).jpg

abschnitte.text: The trial has lasted for years. Braun has spent more than six years in pre-trial detention. In a separate civil case, a Munich court ordered him and two other former executives to pay one hundred and forty million euros in damages. That ruling was not final at the time of this video. As long as there is no criminal verdict, Markus Braun is presumed innocent.
Wirecard's former headquarters in Aschheim is just an office building again. The company was sold off in pieces. Investors lost around twenty billion euros in market value.

bilder.archiv: File:Aschheim-Dornach, Einsteinring 31 v N, 3, ret Wirecard.jpeg

abschnitte.text: But the most uncomfortable lesson is not about one company. It is about a system that wanted to believe. A regulator that went after journalists. Auditors who signed for years. Politicians who were proud of a champion they did not understand.

The people who were right were the ones who were treated as the enemy. So here is the question. Would you have trusted Wirecard in 2018? And who do you think is the next Wirecard? Tell me in the comments. And if you want more stories like this, subscribe.
